To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the color superconducting gap is the key to the formation of hybrid and strange stars and that the energy released during the transition from a metastable hadronic star into the stable hybrid and strange stars is sufficient to power a supernova explosion and/or a gamma-ray burst.

the color superconducting gap can be as large as 10 MeV, the color superconductivity can occur at densities of ~3-4 times the nuclear density, and the quark matter in compact stars can be in a color superconductivity phase.

the formation of color superconducting stars can explain the observed masses and radii, the energy released in the conversion can power supernovae and gamma-ray bursts, and the time delay between the supernovae and the gamma-ray burst is compatible with the observations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of color superconducting phases in the structure of hybrid and quark stars.
a possible connection between supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and the structure of compact stars.
the structure of compact stars, with the possibility of their formation and with the astrophysical consequences of the formation of hybrid or quark compact stars.

the existence of a color superconductor phase is a very promising candidate to explain the recent observations of supernovae and gamma-ray bursts.
a hybrid star or a quark star in a color superconductivity phase could solve the problem of the supernova explosion.
the color superconducting state of quark matter in compact stars can be a viable alternative to the hadronic matter state.

color superconductivity can play a significant role in the structure and formation process of compact stars and that it can provide a possible solution to the supernova explosion problem.

the formation of compact stars is intimately linked to color superconducting phases of quark matter.
